one_liner: Python wheel over a C++20 BS.1770 meter (Nomono's libloudness) that computes integrated LUFS about 1.7x faster than pyebur128/libebur128.
what_it_does: Computes EBU R 128 / ITU BS.1770 integrated loudness (LUFS) of a whole NumPy buffer with one call, loudness.integrated_loudness(samples, sample_rate), for mono (n,) or interleaved (n, channels) float32 input up to 64 channels and 16 Hz to 2.8224 MHz. The Python package exposes only that one function; the vendored C++ core (src/loudness, a C++20 port of libebur128) also has momentary, short-term, loudness range, sample and true peak, median loudness and multi-meter aggregation through a templated loudness::Meter<Mode> class. It is not a drop-in for pyebur128's stateful R128State API or for pyloudnorm's Meter object, but the single-call result is the same quantity.
how_it_is_fast: The K-weighting filter is the same 4th-order combined direct-form-II IIR in double precision as libebur128, so the per-sample recurrence is not faster; the gain comes from the block bookkeeping. libebur128's ebur128_calc_gating_block re-sums the whole 400 ms window of filtered samples at every 100 ms hop (each sample is read four times, strided through an interleaved buffer), while libloudness squares samples into planar per-channel buffers, sums each 100 ms subblock once and forms each gating block from four subblock sums. The input type is a std::variant dispatched once per call, so the integer scaling divisor is a consteval constant (1.0 for float, compiled away) instead of libebur128's runtime static double, and a scoped FTZ/DAZ guard (MXCSR on x86, FPCR on ARM) keeps denormals out of the filter. The Python binding uses Histogram mode, which drops each block's energy into 1000 bins of 0.1 LU instead of keeping a block list.
when_to_use: Batch LUFS measurement of many files or long recordings from Python (dataset normalization, podcast/broadcast QC) where the audio is already a float32 NumPy array; the README run puts 5 minutes of 48 kHz mono at 0.056 s, about 5,360x real time (derived from page data).
Replacing pyloudnorm or torchaudio.functional.loudness on CPU, where the same run is about 5x faster (0.293 s and 0.282 s).

C++20 projects that want an MIT-licensed libebur128-style meter with typed modes and planar or interleaved input: vendor src/loudness (or use upstream nomonosound/libloudness) instead of the Python wrapper.
Multichannel programme loudness with the standard BS.1770 weights: the default map for 5 and 6 channels is L, R, C, (LFE unused), Ls, Rs with 1.41 surround weighting.
when_not_to_use: When you need more than integrated loudness from Python: momentary, short-term, LRA and true peak exist in the C++ core but are not bound (PR #1 adding loudness_per_window has been open since 2025-11-20), so pyebur128 or pyloudnorm stay necessary for those.

When the result must match an exact block-list computation bit for bit: the binding always uses Histogram mode (0.1 LU bins, bin-centre energies), which is within the EBU 0.1 LU tolerance but not identical to libebur128 without EBUR128_MODE_HISTOGRAM.
Streaming or chunked input from Python: each call builds a fresh meter and needs at least 400 ms of audio, so there is no incremental state across calls.

Intel macOS, 32-bit or other platforms without published wheels (PyPI 0.2.0 ships macOS arm64, manylinux/musllinux x86-64 and aarch64, Windows amd64); a source build needs CMake 3.22, a C++20 compiler and the git submodules.
When you expect large wins over libebur128 itself: the measured margin over pyebur128 is about 1.7x from a single run, and the per-sample IIR is identical.

integration.form: module (pybind11 Python extension, wheels on PyPI); the C++ core builds as a static library from src/loudness
integration.dependencies: numpy >= 1.22 at runtime; build needs pybind11 >= 2.12, scikit-build-core >= 0.9.6, CMake >= 3.22, plus vendored gcem and bshoshany/thread-pool (git submodules)
integration.platforms: Wheels for Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (glibc and musl), macOS arm64, Windows x86-64; core is portable C++ with FTZ code for SSE2 and ARM and a manual-FTZ fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Each Python call builds its own meter, so calls are independent, but the binding does not release the GIL, so Python threads serialize. In C++ a Meter instance is not documented as thread-safe; addFramesMT runs true peak per channel and the loudness filter as separate tasks, so it does not parallelize integrated loudness alone.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same integrated LUFS quantity as pyebur128/pyloudnorm from one function call, but a different API and no M/S/LRA/true peak in Python

gotchas: The binding forcecasts to C-contiguous float32: float64 input (soundfile.read's default) is silently copied and rounded to float32, and transposed views are copied, even though the C++ core accepts double, int16 and int32 directly.

Input must be (samples, channels). A channels-first (C, n) array always raises ValueError, because it reads as C frames, under the 400 ms minimum, so torch-style data must be transposed first, which the forcecast turns into a copy.
The vendor/thread-pool submodule URL is SSH (git@github.com:bshoshany/thread-pool.git), so a recursive HTTPS clone without SSH keys fails to fetch it.
Package tests cover only two fixture files at a 0.1 LU tolerance plus argument checks; the EBU Tech 3341/3342 conformance cases live in upstream nomonosound/libloudness, not in this repository.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No other loudness meter is catalogued; the video-audio siblings are codecs, resamplers and analysis toolkits (audioFlux, libsonare, pedalboard), none of which computes BS.1770 integrated loudness. The real alternative is libebur128 itself (via pyebur128): pick this when you only need integrated LUFS from Python and want the faster single call.
verified_claims_summary: scripts/performance_benchmark.py times one call per library with time.time() on 5 minutes of 48 kHz mono float32 uniform white noise: loudness 0.1.0 0.056 s, pyebur128 0.1.1 0.096 s (about 1.7x), torchaudio 2.8.0 0.282 s, pyloudnorm 0.1.1 0.293 s, pyloudness 1.1.2 0.581 s (which includes writing and reading a WAV file). No CPU, OS, compiler or flags are given, there is no warmup or repetition, and loudness runs in Histogram mode while pyebur128 runs in MODE_I block-list mode; that mismatch costs little here (about 3,000 blocks against 14.4 million filtered samples), and pyebur128 takes the float32 buffer without conversion (ebur128_add_frames_float), so the comparison is otherwise like for like.
status_note: Small (33 stars, 68 commits, 0 open issues, one open PR) but maintained, with release 0.2.0 on 2025-12-26 adding Python 3.14 wheels; MIT-licensed, with a C++ core that is easy to vendor.
